title: Omaha Morning Brief
summary: Oil above $100, inflation at 3.7%, a 5.10% ten-year yield, and doubts about how artificial intelligence is being financed.

paragraphs.text: Good morning, Warren.
It is Friday, October 16th.
Four things matter this morning.
Oil is above $100 because of the Iran war.
Inflation is rising again.
Long-term interest rates are above 5%.
And investors have started asking how the artificial intelligence build-out is being paid for.
September consumer prices rose 3.7% from a year earlier, up from 3.4% in August, driven by gasoline.
Core prices, without food and energy, rose 2.6%.
Wholesale prices rose 6.3% over the year, the fastest since 2022.
The Federal Reserve, under Chair Kevin Warsh, raised its rate in September to between 3.75% and 4%, its first increase since 2023.
It meets again October 27 and 28, and futures put the odds of another hike at about one in three.
The 10-year Treasury yield closed at 5.10%.
Three-month Treasury bills pay 4.28%.
The federal deficit for the fiscal year just ended was about $2 trillion.
On Thursday the Dow rose 1.1% to 52,178, and the S&P 500 rose 0.3% to 7,744.
For the week, the S&P is down 0.9% and the Nasdaq is down 2.4%.
The damage is in chips and artificial intelligence.
The Philadelphia semiconductor index has fallen seven days in a row and sits about 12% below its early October peak.
The 20 largest artificial intelligence and chip stocks lost more than $1 trillion of market value this week.
Korea's Kospi fell 7.6% on Thursday alone.
On valuation, the S&P 500 trades at about 19 times expected earnings.
That is an earnings yield near 5.2%, barely above the 10-year Treasury.
Total stock market value is about 238% of gross domestic product, against a long-run average near 168%.
The big banks reported.
JPMorgan earned $5.57 a share, below forecasts, and cut share buybacks to a fraction of its usual pace.
Jamie Dimon said, quote, we can redeploy that capital at very good returns over time.
He said the bank is tightening credit a little, though card losses fell last quarter.
Goldman Sachs earned $17.01 a share against about $13 expected.
Citigroup and Morgan Stanley also beat.
Bank of America missed, and the Treasury fined it $1.2 billion after it admitted willful anti-money-laundering violations.
In artificial intelligence, watch the debt.
CoreWeave, which rents out computing power, carries more than $51 billion of debt and obligations, and the cost of insuring that debt against default hit a record this week.
Oracle fell almost 9% on Wednesday.
It burned $5.4 billion of cash last quarter after $28.5 billion of capital spending.
Meanwhile, Taiwan Semiconductor reported record profit, up 69%.
Elsewhere, UnitedHealth beat and raised its outlook.
Delta cut its profit forecast, and its finance chief said, all of it's fuel.
Hurricane Isaias is estimated at $1 billion to $4 billion of insured losses, which the rating firm AM Best calls an earnings event, not a capital event.
The Iran war, now in its eighth month, is the biggest single force on prices.
Attacks on shipping in the Strait of Hormuz have picked up, and a container ship sank there this week.
The International Energy Agency expects world oil supply to fall 5.8 million barrels a day this year.
Brent crude settled at $105.92.
On Tuesday, during Houthi attacks on Saudi Arabia, Aramco's headquarters in Dhahran was hit.
President Trump says the United States will not strike Iran before the November 3 midterm elections, and that the blockade of Iranian ports stays.
China's September exports rose 36% from a year earlier, for a near-record trade surplus of $133.5 billion.
Its third-quarter growth figure comes Monday, and its pause on rare earth export controls expires November 10.
The International Monetary Fund sees world growth of 3.1% this year with inflation of 4.7%, assuming Hormuz reopens by March.
In India, the cabinet approved selling control of IDBI Bank to Prem Watsa's Fairfax Financial.
Netflix reports Tuesday, Tesla on Wednesday, and American Express is expected Friday.
Coca-Cola reports October 27, the day the Federal Reserve begins its meeting.
That is the briefing.
Have a good day.
